articles.text: Editor: Last Wednesday new school board members took their seats behind the dais and the board elected a new president. I want to offer congratulations to Lindsay Thomasson and Ruchi Medhekar in their new roles. And to Veronica Andersen Thigpen who now, as board president, is well poised to lead the school board in its selection of a new superintendent and as it ushers in an updated mission and vision for the Piedmont School District. The foundation for this time of transition was thoughtfully laid due, in large part, to the leadership, skill, and hard work of the previous board president Cory Smegal (who will continue on the school board for another two years). She has ably guided the school district these last two eventful years. Those who attended meetings no doubt observed her keen ability to zero in on issues and ask hard questions, and witnessed her compassion for our entire school community when she provided reports to calm, challenge, unite, and inspire us all. There is also much more that Cory did behind the scenes. She asked questions, verified facts, and sought to gain an understanding of issues through research and countless conversations with parents, administrators, educators, staff, students, other board members, as well as educational leaders outside of Piedmont. Cory encouraged board members to share thoughts and ideas and engage in authentic dialogue during meetings. She set a positive tone for these conversations by her ability to be direct while respectful, to disagree and also take time to listen and consider other perspectives. Because of this, Cory can take a great deal of credit for the way we were able to operate as a governance team with civility and transparency at a time when many boards of neighboring school districts were splintered. Always at the heart of Cory’s work on the board has been her deep care for and commitment to our students. We all witnessed her emotion when we heard heartbreaking stories of their mental health issues, her passion for girls’ equality in sports, or her desire to support all students in our schools. She has been no less of a driving force when advocating within the board to support our teachers and staff, or when meeting with state officials to lobby for an increase in funding for public schools. Her strong beliefs drove her perseverance to help the district honestly face district challenges and strive to make changes to meet the changing needs of our students. I am so grateful to have had the privilege to work with Cory, especially while I was vice president and she as president. I know that the board is, once again, in capable hands to help the district to progress and thrive with Veronica Andersen Thigpen at the helm as president. -Megan Pillsbury, for School Board member 1139 Oakland Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611 Phone: 652-2051 • email: news@piedmont-post.com Publisher & Editor: Gray Cathrall City Editor: Jay Russell PRODUCTION MANAGER Victor Cheng REPORTERS Selen Ozturk Ed Gilligan Will Becker (intern) Sohrab “Seb” Ford (intern) SCHOOLS Ada Cliff SPORTS Jonathan Comeaux B. articles.text: Over the past three weeks, mudslides, flooding, and falling trees have become a frequent sight in Piedmont as the city has had to deal with repeated storms – most recently, last weekend’s heavy rain. Speaking on his experience mitigating the damage, Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales said that “Storms are like a test: It’s how we see where the things we do to address these events proactively are working and where they’re not.” The creek cleanup crews included eight Public Works staff working around the clock, along with three on-call contractors, to clear Piedmont’s waterways during the heavy rains from December 30 to January 2. With the more intermittent recent rains, however – like the storm bringing one to two inches of rain to the Bay last weekend, January 13 and 14 – Gonzales said, “we typically only have two staff members out monitoring creeks and clearing inlets at any given time, though there are always more crew on call if something significant occurs — when they can’t remove a large tree from the trash racks.” “If debris like branches and trees are flushed down waterways and not removed,” he emphasized, “the water will flood houses and roadways rather than flowing downhill.” While storm drain inlets throughout Piedmont are regularly being cleared, they’re operating at full capacity. This owes to the fact that the debris catch basins of the drains “were installed 50 to 70 years ago — not up to today’s standards.” Either the grates are too small, whereby any branch washed into the drain could obstruct it entirely, or else the drain itself is too small. Trash rack at foot of Bushy Dell Creek in Piedmont Park Photo by Public Works Dept. Bushy Dell Creek runs full during recent rainstorms. While Gonzales affirmed that the city’s storm system experienced no significant issues over the past three weeks, “they have identified the portions of the system we could proactively change — mainly height, size, and knowing where the drain system’s pressure points are and where we need staffing the most when branches and trees do fall.” “Four fairly significantly sized trees fell as a result of the storm,” he added. One was an 80-foot pine knocked down in Piedmont Park on December 30; another was a Sequoia Redwood split by lightning on Crocker Avenue near Crocker Park on January 10; and a third was a Eucalyptus tree which fell onto communication wires by the Wallace, Winsor and Wildwood Avenue intersection. As a result of the latter incident, Comcast and AT&T lines were out for a day and a half, and the road was not fully cleared until a Comcast crew arrived the next evening. “Nevertheless,” said Gonzales, “our city has 8,000 to 9,000 trees. The fact that we have lost 12 in this storm at our last count” — January 11 — “is a good rate, all things considered.” Public Works has since identified a tree leaning in Piedmont Park which, “while not fallen, is not safe. We plan to bring it down proactively, and continue identifying other potential dangers as the storms continue.” “In Public Works, if you’re doing your job, the damage you face isn’t nearly as involving as maintenance and cleanup,” said Gonzales. “While these storms have really been testing Piedmont’s storm systems, that’s certainly been the case here.” Those with questions about the storm damage and mitigation in Piedmont can email Daniel Gonzales at dgonzales@piedmont.ca.gov, or call him at (510) 420-3061. The talk is co-sponsored by the League of Women Voters and Piedmont Connect. The talk will include an audience question and answer session. California depends on groundwater for up to 60% of its annual supply in times of drought. The SGMA was enacted in 2014 to halt overdraft and bring groundwater basins into balanced levels of pumping and recharge. Under SGMA, basins must reach sustainability within 20 years of implementing their plans. This owes to the fact that the debris catch basins of the drains “were installed 50 to 70 years ago — not up to today’s standards.” Either the grates are too small, whereby any branch washed into the drain could obstruct it entirely, or else the drain itself is too small. Trash rack at foot of Bushy Dell Creek in Piedmont Park Photo by Public Works Dept. Bushy Dell Creek runs full during recent rainstorms. While Gonzales affirmed that the city’s storm system experienced no significant issues over the past three weeks, “they have identified the portions of the system we could proactively change — mainly height, size, and knowing where the drain system’s pressure points are and where we need staffing the most when branches and trees do fall.” “Four fairly significantly sized trees fell as a result of the storm,” he added. One was an 80-foot pine knocked down in Piedmont Park on December 30; another was a Sequoia Redwood split by lightning on Crocker Avenue near Crocker Park on January 10; and a third was a Eucalyptus tree which fell onto communication wires by the Wallace, Winsor and Wildwood Avenue intersection. As a result of the latter incident, Comcast and AT&T lines were out for a day and a half, and the road was not fully cleared until a Comcast crew arrived the next evening. “Nevertheless,” said Gonzales, “our city has 8,000 to 9,000 trees. The fact that we have lost 12 in this storm at our last count” — January 11 — “is a good rate, all things considered.” Public Works has since identified a tree leaning in Piedmont Park which, “while not fallen, is not safe. We plan to bring it down proactively, and continue identifying other potential dangers as the storms continue.” “In Public Works, if you’re doing your job, the damage you face isn’t nearly as involving as maintenance and cleanup,” said Gonzales. “While these storms have really been testing Piedmont’s storm systems, that’s certainly been the case here.” Those with questions about the storm damage and mitigation in Piedmont can email Daniel Gonzales at dgonzales@piedmont.ca.gov, or call him at (510) 420-3061. articles.text: The Piedmont Appreciating Diversity Film Series continues tomorrow, Thursday, January 19, with a free screening of the documentary Through the Night. Childcare, who needs it? Everyone. If you are a parent, grandparent and/or community member, you know that society can’t function without it. High quality, dependable and affordable childcare is the essential service necessary to every family and to the American workforce and yet it is always a struggle to find. If you are a doctor, nurse, police officer or in a myriad of other work sectors such as transportation or hospitality, you know the additional challenge in finding night care. This important topic is brought to life in a powerful, uplifting documentary film, Through the Night, directed by Loira Limbal. The film is an intimate cinema verite portrait of working mothers whose lives intersect at a 24-hour daycare center: a mother working the overnight shift as an essential worker at a pediatric hospital, another holding 3 jobs to support her family and an amazing woman (Nunu) who, for over 2 decades, has cared for the children whose parents have nowhere else to turn. A tender portrait of strength, love, and selflessness, Through the Night showcases the multiplicity of “women’s work”-paid, underpaid, and unpaid--all while negotiating the terms of a dignified existence under the 3 arrows of racism, sexism, and capitalism in America. The screening is at 7 p.m., followed by a short talk and Q & A with Kym Johnson, Executive Director of Bananas, Inc., an early care and education organization that provides resources for families and child care providers to support and educate our youngest Ellen Driscoll Playhouse is at Havens School, 325 Highland Avenue.

articles.text: Max Rivera “Climate anxiety” refers to persistent fear, worry or distress linked to uncertainty about the future in a changing climate. The term has also been defined as a chronic fear of environmental doom. Given that teens and young adults are more likely to witness the worsening effects of climate change in their lifetime, it’s not surprising that many young people are affected by climate anxiety. A 10-country survey of 10,000 young people ages 16 to 25 published in the medical journal The Lancet showed that climate change and inadequate responses by governments and previous generations are associated with climate anxiety in young people globally. Of those surveyed, 83% believed that people have failed to care for the planet and 75% believed that the future is frightening. Hana Thomas, a junior at Piedmont High School, said that climate change “sparks a lot of anxiety for my generation.” She also feels climate anxiety personally: “In all my visions for the future,” she said, “there’s this voice in the back of my head saying this could all be impossible if we don’t stop climate change. It definitely affects big life choices, like do I want to have children, do I want to bring children into a world like this? These are conversations I have with my friends, even at age 16, because it feels like there is so little action on such a big issue.” Piedmont High classmate Max Rivera first learned about the severity of climate change as a fifth grader in science class. “I’m still looking forward to possible changes people can make towards helping the environment and limiting climate change,” he said, “but I know that my life is going to be impacted by this pressing [issue]. If we don’t act now, it’s going to be impacting more people later on in life.” Young people who are concerned about climate change often feel powerless. Of those surveyed in the study published in The Lancet, 65% believed furthermore that we are failing young people and 58% believed that people in power are betraying youth and future generations. “I’m putting all the hope I have of fixing climate change into people of power, like the government, and I don’t know if I necessarily trust that their actions will really be reflected as beneficial to everyone including the environment,” Rivera said. Along those lines, Thomas expressed her wish that older generations felt climate anxiety as deeply as young people do, because it would inspire action. “It’s my generation’s problem now, even though we have done very little to worsen the effects of Hana Thomas it,” she said. Nevertheless, many young people are turning their climate anxiety into action. According to a partnership survey between the Washington Post and the Kaiser Family Foundation, about 1 in 4 American teens have participated in a walkout, attended a rally, or written to a public official about climate change. Thomas herself began interning for Youth vs Apocalypse when she was in middle school. She has since helped to organize climate marches in San Francisco and she currently interns with Undaunted K-12, an organization whose mission is to support public schools in transitioning to zero emissions. She plans on majoring in environmental studies in college. Rivera is the co-president of Piedmont High School’s Green Club whose goal is to “spread awareness about climate change and other environmental issues. “By spreading awareness and acting on these issues that are present, we can make Piedmont and surrounding areas and our community a better place overall,” he said. articles.text: Photo by Sohrab “Seb” Ford Millennium High School senior Samiya Jones (left) and freshman Tobias Del Bono walk to class Millennium High School (MHS) was given its name in 2000. It had existed earlier under the name Piedmont Independent High School. Under the new name and leadership of Principal Ken Yale, it became a school designed to serve students within Piedmont and the broader Bay Area who would benefit from a non-competitive, personalized education that traditional high schools don’t provide. After 22 years of fostering a wonderful space for its students to grow, it is time to acknowledge and appreciate Millennium High school. The small high school with roughly 70 students actively works to ensure that its class structure and grading systems promote a democratic and safe environment for students to flourish. Inside MHS classrooms, teachers and administrators encourage students to share their unique voices and participate in constructive group activities. Under the school’s motto “Respect, Impact, Skills, and Engage” (R.I.S.E.), students are asked to take responsibility for their personal lives and in the school community. Students are expected to be actively working towards goals and benefitting the whole, whether in monthly “Falcon Meetings,” which brings the entire student body together for a conversation, the school’s leadership class, or seeking and engaging in extracurricular opportunities. Students are also asked to take ownership of their schedules. Just like Piedmont High School (PHS) students, MHS students must fulfill the “University of California A-G” requirements to graduate. Unlike PHS, Millennium creates a space for students to customize how they meet these requirements. Students can gain credit through college courses, community service, electives at PHS, internships, and work experience. This allows students to work as fast as they want in order to achieve their full potential. Due to the school’s encouragement of community participation, MHS has formed a safe space for students to engage with one another. Outside of the standards of traditional high schools, students can truly enjoy learning and companionship without the stress of competition. “I love just feeling welcome and safe and just happy to be at school,” said Shybrea Ottaviano a sophomore at MHS, “I’ve never really been excited to go to school before. pages.text: 10 Wednesday, January 18, 2023 CRYSTAL’S REFLECTIONS By Crystal Vacker This adventure actually started the week before winter break. I was being driven home from an end-of-season tennis banquet at my school, when my father told me that something had happened – but I shouldn’t worry about it. I guess he wanted me to not get too panicked before I even got home. The faded streetlights by highway 24 led us home as the world around us descended into darkness. Finally home, it was revealed that after decades of functioning, our washer and dryer unit had passed on. As a parting gift, half of the house and our basement were flooded. At our house it’s not entirely uncommon for something to suddenly stop working and wreak havoc – but this was on a completely new level. My mother had wanted a new laundry room for quite some time, though never under these circumstances. She had turned on the machine, something she had done countless time before, and left the house to run some errands. Four hours later, as she sat in the kitchen making a cup of coffee she noticed a stream of water making its way out of the utility room with the washer and dryer and into the kitchen. The machine was still cycling, Winter Break from Hell and the sound was a bit unusual. When she ran to the basement, she encountered a mini Niagara Falls, with water roaring down from the ceiling and into the basement. Apparently, the machine had become stuck on the “extra rinse” cycle, and had been pumping water into the basement for hours. And in a twist of cruel fate, the storm drain had been clogged by leaves that fell during the previous night’s windstorm. Water was up to her knees, and one can only imagine the effort it took to unclog the drain and then deal with the flood inside the house. A handyman was called. He was able to turn the washer off…but the chaos continued. First, several huge industrial-size dryers had to be brought into the house and left on for 24 hours for several days. They were loud and relentless, as if someone was constantly blow-drying a giant’s head. At the same time our fridge decided to take a vacation. It suddenly stopped working, and all the workers we asked to help couldn’t fix it. They told us it would be a ridiculous amount of money to fix, and never got back to us. Luckily, we had a backup fridge in the garage. Then came time for a decision: what type of new floors did we want? To repair the water damage, workers tore up 75 years’ worth of layers of linoleum. One of the layers, a geometrical linoleum, I actually quite liked and lobbied to keep that throughout the laundry room and kitchen, but nobody shared my retro design vision. My mother was set on tile and convinced my father, who wasn’t particularly excited to spend his Christmas break listening to the sound of tile being cut, but she told him it would look stunning. So. of course he agreed. The problem with tile is that it’s fragile. If my mother bangs pots and pans on it, like one can do on a wooden floor, she would crack that tile in no time. My mother dismissed my concern, but I could see that her determination for tile was someone dented (pardon the pun). Two stores and several hours later, with no floor type found and low morale, it seemed like there was no hope. But as we drove home in despair, I jokingly pointed out a store which we passed hundreds of times on our way to and from Piedmont Ballet, aptly named Simple Floors. Simple Floors saved us. It had a perfect floor – waterproof wood that looked like tile. The material could be picked up and installed within the next few days. Our kitchen had never looked so good. Oddly, around the same time the refrigerator which had gone on a vacation started working again. At first we didn’t believe it, so we only moved a couple things from the other fridge, but the fridge in the kitchen kept cold. One could only wonder what it was up to. Then came what should have been an exciting part: buying a new washer and dryer. But in our household, one never knows. First, my mother insisted that we drive all the way to Pleasant Hill, because she didn’t want to go to Best Buy in Emeryville. Once we arrived in Pleasant Hill we were greeted by a torrential downpour. My mother and sister proceeded to inspect every machine in the store and listen to lengthy explanations of the salesperson, which only seemed to confuse them further. Meanwhile my dad and I walked around aimlessly figuring that our opinion didn’t really matter. Finally, the choice was made and the installation arranged for the day before the New Year. Then my father jokingly asked my mother how she would reach the bottom of the tall washing machine. She’s only 5-4, but the question sent her into a panic attack. For the next 10 minutes we all demonstrated how she would get the clothes from below. It was quite the show to other parking lot visitors. Not until the machines arrived and were installed on the promised day did my mother calm down. So now, with the f loor redone, the walls repainted, the machines put in their rightful place, the reborn fridge washed, the house fixed, one could kick back and relax, right? Wrong. That same day, our car decided on its own to continuously run the fan – even after the engine was turned off. What followed was an expensive trip on New Year’s Eve, the 31st of December. But we got it fixed and finally there was peace and quiet in our household. And then the rain came and our basement flooded, this time with rainwater. It was unclogged right away with a broom. A few days later my sister went back to college, and I have been on flood watch ever since. On January 3rd, I went back to school, hoping that all these incidents weren’t going to become a trend for the new year. And despite the revenge of the appliances, I had a great break. I got to spend time with my sister, I hung out with friends, and enjoyed an amazing Christmas. Crystal Vacker is a Piedmont resident and a sophomore at Bentley School in Lafayette. articles.text: PHS beats Alameda, St. Mary’s, loses to Oakland High Piedmont High’s boys’ basketball team wrapped up a strong week of action, defeating Alameda 59-57 at home on Thursday, January 12, beating St. Mary’s 65-38 at an MLK Showcase at Berkeley High on Saturday, January 14, and losing to top-ranked Oakland High 73-57 at the MLK Day Classic at Merritt College on Monday, January 16. The wins over Alameda and St. Mary’s extended Piedmont’s winning streak to four games before playing the highly touted Oakland High squad, which came in as SportStar Magazine’s No. 20 ranked team in NorCal. Piedmont’s win over Alameda was the highlight of the week, with sophomore Ravi Silverberg scoring the game winner on a 3-pointer in the closing seconds for a 59-57 win. “The wins over Alameda and St. Mary’s were awesome, I think our defense in the second quarter against St. Mary’s was the best we’ve played all season. The Alameda buzzer-beater was another great win; our guys were ready for the critical moment. Playing Oakland High is great for us. Playing teams like this gets you ready for late in the season,” said coach Ben Spencer. The victory over the Hornets put Piedmont in first place in the Western Alameda County Conference (WACC) with a 3-0 record ahead of Berkeley (3-1), San Leandro (2-1), Alameda (2-1), and O’Dowd (2-2). With nine of the 10 remaining games against league opponents, the focus is now to become the WACC’s first champion other than Bishop O’Dowd since the league’s inception. The Dragons have won all 10 league titles of the WACC’s existence, sharing first-place honors with San Leandro in 2016 and 2019. Piedmont plays at O’Dowd today, Wednesday, January 18, and at Berkeley on Friday, January 20. “Wednesday will be a great test for us. They (O’Dowd) will play a similar style to Oakland High. Our guards now know what to expect,” said Spencer. 59-57 thriller over Alameda In a heated win over Alameda, Piedmont led 12-8 to end the Staff Photos Ravi Silverberg scored the game-winning 3-pointer against Alameda, putting Piedmont on top of the WACC. first quarter and 27-21 by halftime. The Hornets cut the deficit to 39-38 by the end of the third quarter, and the two sides traded points back and forth down to the wire. With Alameda clinging to a 57-56 lead in the waning seconds, Silverberg moved the ball up court. He kicked the ball inside to Harris, who passed to Matteo Costa after a couple of dribbles. Costa then drove inside, stopped, and turned to pass outside to Silverberg. The sophomore guard instinctively put up the 3-pointer, draining it as time expired. Final scorers: Harris scored 18 points, Silverberg scored 14, Brit Burden had 10, Declan Linnane scored eight, while Costa and Thorin Holmes had four. 65-38 victory over St. Mary’s The game was the first time Piedmont and St. Mary’s have faced each other since the North Coast Section championship won by Piedmont in 2020. The Highlanders trailed 10-5 at the end of the first quarter and then exploded for 28 points in the second to lead 33-20 at the half. PHS extended its lead to 51-31 in the third period and closed out with 14 points in the fourth for the 65-38 victory. Final scorers: Harris led with 17 points, Theo Evans had 10, Burden and Silverberg scored nine, Holmes had eight, while Cairo Osman, Teagan Haddawy, Costa and Linnane had three. A.J. Harris scored 37 points against Oakland High, 18 in a game with Alameda, and 17 points against St. Mary’s.

Make no mistake about it; Piedmont High’s girls’ basketball team is well on its way as being recognized as of the best squads in the state. Currently holding SportsStar Magazine’s No. 1 ranking in NorCal, the Highlanders toppled No. 5 ranked Salesian by six points, 69-63, on Monday, January 16, at Bishop O’Dowd’s MLK Day Showcase. Over the past week, Piedmont also defeated Cathedral Catholic of San Diego 80-37 on Saturday, January 14, at St. Mary’s of Stockton in its MLK Showcase. Earlier, on Thursday, January 12, they overwhelmed league opponent Alameda 73-14. Facing Salesian, the Highlanders had to overcome a lot after three starters had to leave the game early. Guard Adrienne Blackwell suffered an injury in the first quarter, and two players fouled out. Guard Perseas Gioukaris fouled out in the third quarter, and with a 13-point lead midway through the fourth quarter, forward Eva Levingston, its leading scorer, fouled out. It required big contributions from role players Shakila Zuberi and Katarina Melian. “I definitely think it wasn’t our best game and we could’ve played more aggressively. But, we pulled it out and it was a fun game,” said team captain, senior Trinity Zamora, who finished with 18 points. “Close games like this show us who we really are. We changed up our defense coming out of the first half and were just being more patient and smart with the ball.” Piedmont’s win moved its record to 15-0, the best start since the era of the celebrity Paris twins in _____. articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ soccer team had a tough week with two consecutive league losses on the road. They lost 3-2 at Castro Valley on Wednesday, January 11 and 1-0 at Berkeley on Friday, January 13. “We looked rusty, to be honest,” said coach Dan Chubbock following the loss to Berkeley. “We worked hard and tried hard, but we lacked quality. There’s no shame to losing to these teams. Today, we just couldn’t break them down.” The pair of games brings the Highlanders’ record to 5-0-3 overall and 3-0-2 in league (W-TL), placing them third. Berkeley’s win jolted them to first-place at 4-0-1, while Castro Valley is in second at 3-1-1. Despite the losses the matches revealed how close the WACC’s Foothill Division is. Castro Valley recently tied San Leandro 1-1, a team which PHS beat 6-1 one week earlier. Berkeley, meanwhile, lost to Bishop O’Dowd 2-1 on January 6, and Piedmont beat the Dragons 1-0 on December 7. “We’re looking to bounce back. It’s tough after taking any loss, especially when these girls believe they can win the league. Now we have to beat Berkeley, Castro Valley, and pretty much go undefeated the rest of the season. Everyone has beaten everyone,” explained Chubbock. 1-0 loss to Berkeley Berkeley did well against Piedmont to sit defensively and not allow clear looks on the middle of the pitch. They pressured the Highlanders when they entered the zone to force loose balls up field. The Jackets’ goal in the 28th minute came after the referee called a handball outside of the box on Piedmont. The Berkeley goalie Polzin took the free kick a foot above the penalty area, arching her ball to the far post for the eventual game-winner in the 28th minute. articles.text: Piedmont Middle School’s championship basketball team included (front) Sophia Puckett (left), Lauren Udovch, Cory Minor, Carly Kemp-Malone, Madeline Lee, Elly Mak, Maggie Eidt, Edie Elmquist; (top) Nicole Li, Cora Borzowski Schrade, Izara Dando, Olivia Humphries, Olivia Stevens, Lucy Dorsey, Ella Thomason, and Hannah Joerger. Describing a sports team as a sum greater than its parts has become a cliché for good reason: seeing a group of individuals band together to accomplish something they couldn’t individually is always rewarding. Those who watched the Piedmont Middle School girls’ basketball team this season got that reward. The Scots finished their season with a sterling 10-2 record, capitalized by winning a four-team end-of-season tournament hosted by King Middle School in Berkeley. The season was marked by incredible individual and team improvement overseen by head coach Maddie Mills and assistant coach Michael Love. The team demonstrated a season-long commitment to playing with effort and intensity. The Scots were overflowing with team camaraderie, and no play occurred without cheers or words of encouragement from the players on the bench. The Scots won their first game of the season against Walnut Creek Intermediate, and followed a tough loss to Joaquin Moraga with a narrow 20-17 road win against Stanley Intermediate of Lafayette. Point guard Olivia Stevens showed her talent and poise during this pre-Thanksgiving stretch. The 16-player team showed their strength by dividing and conquering in two separate games scheduled at the same time. The team of the hard-charging Elly Mak and Lauren Udovch defeated Willard, while a second team of fierce rebounder Hannah Joerger held MLK to only four points in a win. Sharpshooter Olivia Humphries sank threes all season and scored 14 points in Piedmont’s 15-10 win over Stanley. Improvement became apparent at this point in the season; Lucy Dorsey’s hustle, Edie Elmquist’s ferocity, and Ella Thomasson’s defense and rebounding started to shine. Nicole Li’s all-around game and Maggie Eidt’s screening and passing were highlights all season as well. The Scots earned another victory over Walnut Creek Intermediate before losing to Joaquin Moraga before beating Head Royce in a preview of the tournament to come at MLK. Piedmont had reason to feel confident heading into the tournament. Carly Kemp-Malone and Cora Borzowski were among the players continuing to compete hard in practice and in games. Izara Dando and Sophia Puckett and their fantastic attitudes made them valued members of the team. The Scots had already beaten MLK and Head Royce, still nothing was easy. The team had to overcome multiple time changes and a frigid gym in order to win the tournament. Starting slowly in their first game against Head Royce, they were spurred on by the defense and energy of Madeline Lee and Cory Minor in the win. The first-round game was close, but Piedmont ensured the championship round wasn’t competitive as they beat MLK to earn the victory in the tournament. The team then capped their season with a 36-4 triumph over Black Pine Circle. The Scots had a roster of mostly 7th graders, two 6th and one 8th grader.

articles.text: SOREN DIXON Soccer & Lacrosse With an enrollment of roughly 900 students, you will often see athletes at Piedmont High playing more than one sport. Here is a feature on some influential athletes competing in multiple sports. Soren Dixon, a senior, is a key starter on Piedmont’s soccer and lacrosse teams. On the soccer pitch, Dixon is a defender in Todd Sullivan’s system and is a leading scorer on the lacrosse team. As a junior in 2022, Dixon was a captain of the lacrosse team’s sixth-consecutive WACC Championship. In the championship game against Bishop O’Dowd, Dixon scored four goals in a 10-9 win and earned first-team AllLeague honors. Dixon also helped Piedmont’s soccer team win last year’s Shoreline title with an undefeated league record of 10-0-0. He helped their defense keep a clean sheet in a 1-0 shutout of University and led lead the team to the school’s first-ever Div. 4 North Coast Section NCS Championship. Staff Photos Peter Krumins is a two-sport athlete on water polo and baseball. He was The Posts’ 2022 Sophomore of the Year. PETER KRUMINS Water Polo & Baseball Peter Krumins, a junior, is a leading player on the water polo team in the fall and baseball team in the spring. He’s already won three WACC championships, with two consecutive titles in water polo and as a member of the defending Shoreline champion baseball team. This past fall Krumins helped lead the Highlanders to its second WACC title by scoring six goals in the 13-4 win over Alameda on October 29. He was also a key player in Piedmont’s 2021 WACC title, the first in school history, in which he where he scored twice in a 12-8 win over Berkeley. On the baseball diamond last spring, Krumins started at third base and hit for a stellar .324 average, with 22 hits, three doubles, three triples, and a home run. In the league championship 6-5 win over Encinal, he was 2-for-4 with two runs scored, while also having one hit and one run scored in Piedmont’s 4-3 NCS opening round win over St. Patrick, and adding another hit and run scored in the NCS 6-5 loss to St. Joseph. The Post named Krumins the Sophomore of the Year in 2022. Friedie Schickedanz is a two-sport athlete on water polo and lacrosse. FRIEDIE SCHICKEDANZ Water Polo & Lacrosse Friedie Schickedanz is a senior and a two-sport athlete in water polo and lacrosse. She is a two-year starter as the water polo goalie and played on the varsity lacrosse team last spring. In water polo, Schickedanz led Piedmont to a fifth-place finish in the league tournament by recording 11 saves in a 13-12 sudden-death overtime win over Berkeley, including three clutch saves in overtime. In the spring, Schickedanz scored in a 14-9 game with Tamalpais in lacrosse. Piedmont finished went 4-1 against league opponents, and lost in the first round of the North Coast Section playoffs. Soren Dixon is a key player on both the soccer and lacrosse teams.

articles.text: Former PHS player advances to 3rd round of Australian Ope We’re in January now, meaning it’s the start of the ATP Tennis Tour’s Grand Slam lineup and the Australian Open underway. Former Piedmont High player Mackie McDonald made his sixth appearance in the main draw of the Aussie Open, making his way to the second round after defeating 21-year-old American Brandon Nakashima and then pulling off a stunning upset of one of the world’s greatest players, Rafael Nadal. Against Nakashima, McDonald won a heated match in five sets, which included three sets going to 7-point tiebreakers, 7-6 (7-5), 7-6 (7-1), 1-6, 7-6 (12-10), 6-4. In the match with Nadal, McDonald led 6-4, 5-3 before the No. 1 ranked player exited the match. Nadal re-entered the match to make it 5-4, but McDonald won with set-point, 6-4. McDonald, 27, is currently No. 64 overall on the ATP Tennis Tour and should improve after defeating No. 46 Nakashima and going stride-for-stride with Nadal. Mackie won the first set 6-4 after taking set-point when forcing deuce and gaining advantage, leading 4-1 at one point in the set. You could see what it meant to him, beaming a smile during a successful first set victory against when of the best players of all time. McDonald stole the first game of the second set as the returner with three break-point opportunities and then went up 2-0 as the server. He nearly took the third game of the second set as the returner by forcing deuce and briefly having advantage, but Nadal powered through. Nadal tied 2-2 as the returner and then went ahead 3-2. McDonald tied 3-3 and then went ahead 4-3 as the returner forcing deuce and taking advantage, once again. McDonald then went up 5-3, and Nadal wound up hampered by a nagging hip injury. Mackie smashed two straight aces and Nadal went to the bench with an injury. Nadal returned after a medical timeout to make it 5-4 but McDonald won as the Photos courtesy of Australian Open Twitter Mackie McDonald is set to play in the third round of the Australian Open after a shocking upset of No. 1 Rafael Nadal. returner, 6-4, closing out the second set. In the third set, Nadal regained some form. The two players traded games as server until the set was at 5-5. From there, McDonald went ahead 6-5 as the returner up with two break point opportunities up 40-15. With match point, Mackie closed out the biggest match of his life

articles.text: Oakland Museum of California (OMCA) has celebrated Lunar New Year for over two decades with a day of festivities, art, music and dance. This year’s event, honoring the Year of the Rabbit on Sunday, January 29, is the museum’s 22nd annual Lunar New Year celebration. Festivities begin at 11 a.m. At noon at the outdoor garden stage, a lucky lion dance will be performed by Developing Virtue Secondary School students and kick off a series of events. Events at the outdoor garden stage include: 12:30–1:00 p.m. – Nanta Drum Play and Pan-Gut by Hansamo’s Nanta, Pungmulnori & Dance Teams 1:15–1:45 p.m. – Vietnamese 16-string đàn tranh (zither) performance by Vân-Ánh Võ 2:00–2:30 p.m. – Filipino Singkil dance performance and lesson by Earlene Escobal and the Pilipinx American Student Association at CSU East Bay 2:45–3:00 p.m. – Malaysian 24 Seasons Drumming by Developing Virtue Secondary School 3:15–3:35 p.m. – Street style dance performance and lesson by Str8jacket, as seen on America’s Got Talent The celebration concludes at 3:45 p.m. with a dragon dance performed by Developing Virtue Secondary School students. articles.text: Year of the Rabbit family fun day is February 5 San Francisco’s Asian Art Museum invites everyone to celebrate the Year of the Rabbit in this year’s Lunar New Year event on Sunday, February 5, when the museum will host an array of family-friendly activities. Lunar New Year, sometimes called Chinese New Year, is celebrated widely in China but also in Tibet, Japan, Korea, Thailand, and here in the Bay Area. Festivities involve honoring ancestors and making preparations for a prosperous and joyous new year. The rabbit is the fourth in the 12-year cycle of animals that appear in the Chinese zodiac. Online activities Families can visit the Asian Art Museum’s website for printable coloring sheets related to the Year of the Rabbit, as well as an instructional page on how to create your own Lunar New Year red envelope. You can also watch youth dancers from dance company LionDanceMe perform a New Year Lion dance, a traditional way to ring in the new year. You can also view “At the Table Dumpling Adventure’’ with Kristina Cho. Cho is a food stylist and blogger who shows her technique for making traditional Chinese pork and shrimp dumplings, a common dish for any time of the year. Cho is the author of the cookbook “Mooncakes and Milk Bread,” which includes the recipe for these dumplings and other traditional dishes. Family fun day The Asian Art Museum will have storytelling and family-friendly Lunar New Year activities. Art activities will begin at 11 a.m., in which children and adults will learn about traditional Chinese art. Storytellers include Fred Sheng (“Why the Rat Comes First”), Miriam Mills (“The Tet Pole”), and Leta Bushyhead (“Nian, the Beast”). Visit https://asianart.org/cultural-celebrations/celebrate-lunar-new-year/ for a full schedule and to purchase tickets. SF marks Lunar New Year with public display of large statues The city of San Francisco is celebrating the Year of the Rabbit with large, colorful rabbit statues placed in five locations: the Chase Center, Chinatown-Rose Pak Station, Union Square, Lucky Supermarket on Sloat Boulevard, and the Asian Art Museum. The project is sponsored by the Chinese Chamber of Commerce.
articles.title: Asian Art Museum celebrates Lunar New Year

articles.text: A photo exhibit, The New Black Vanguard: Photography between Art and Fashion, is now on view at The Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD) in San Francisco through March 5. The exhibition is having its West Coast premiere at MoAD and highlights the work of 15 contemporary fashion photographers from London, Lagos, New York, Johannesburg, and more. Each artist’s work showcases a fresh perspective on fashion, beauty, race, gender, and aesthetics. The New Black Vanguard is curated by Antwaun Sargent and organized by Aperture, New York. Visitors will see over 100 select works from international artists and photographers, including Tyler Mitchell, the first Black photographer hired to shoot a cover story for American Vogue. To learn more and to purchase tickets to MoAD, visit https:// www.moadsf.org/exhibitions/thenew-black-vanguard. ®
articles.title: The New Black Vanguard exhibit at MoAD through March

articles.text: Photo by Joan Marcus Uzo Aduba and Ron Jones appear in Berkeley Rep’s production of Clyde, opening this Friday, January 20 Berkeley Repertory Theatre will premiere a production of Clyde, a play by Lynn Nottage, opening this Friday, January 20. Nottage’s newest play was nominated for a 2022 Tony Award for Best Play. The twotime Pulitzer Prize-winning playwright describes it as a “feelgood comedic drama” in a story that follows formerly incarcerated kitchen staff at a truck-stop sandwich shop who attempt to rebuild their lives. The staff’s demanding boss aims to sidetrack their dreams when each staff member is asked by a mysterious chef to imagine and then create the perfect sandwich. The play opened on Broadway in November 2021 to favorable reviews. Berkeley Rep’s production is directed by Taylor Reynolds, in co-production with Huntington Theatre Company. Post-show discussions will be held on February 3, 9, and 14, led by members of Berkeley Rep’s staff. To purchase tickets, visit https:// www.berkeleyrep.org/shows/ clyde-s/.

articles.text: Michael Stehr presents lecture on Impressionists at Center for the Arts on Feb. 3 Local artist and art historian Michael Stehr will offer an illustrated lecture at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Friday, February 3, titled “A Stroll Through the Musée’ d’Orsay: An Evening with the Impressionists.” Doors open at 6 p.m. and the lecture will begin at 6:30 p.m. The lecture celebrates one of the great museums of the world. Some regard the Impressionist movement that began in Paris in the second half of the 1800’s to be the most important movement in art history since the Renaissance. Indeed, the Impressionists marked the departure from the oppressive constraints of traditional painting while serving as a stepping stone in the evolution towards becoming “modern.” The broken brush strokes and vaporous colors associated with the movement have these pictures being some of the most widely appreciated in Western art. For those cherishing the art of the Impressionists, there is one ultimate destination to enjoy these remarkable paintings: the Musée d’Orsay in Paris. Join art historian Michael Stehr as he makes Michael Stehr and Musee d’Orsay group visit director Sandrine Bourbon a return visit to Piedmont Center for the Arts to guide visitors on a virtual stroll through this brilliant museum. Tickets are $20 per at the door; cash only. For more information, contact Michael Stehr at mstehrart@gmail.com. Proof of vaccination will be required indoors. The story is based on a piece of 2015 investigative journalism by Jessica Pressler, which appeared in New York Magazine. The narrative focuses, at least initially, on two women, one the veteran Ramona (Jennifer Lopez), and the newbie, Dorothy, aka Destiny (Constance Wu). At first, Ramona agrees to teach Destiny the club workarounds. And in one long scene, she demonstrates the art of delivering a very hot, seductive pole dance that will, she insists, cause the raucous clients to shower the stage with money. It’s actually a moment of stunning athleticism by Lopez that defies her age of 50. After a few weeks working together, and Destiny proving her chops, Ramona suggests that the Wall Street hustlers who show up with pockets of cash, and credit cards to match, can be scammed. The rationale is that they scam their marks all day (this is early 2000s) and now it’s their turn. All they have to do, with the aid of a drug, dropped into the men’s drinks, lift from their pockets their plastic credit cards, max them out, and while they’re sleeping it off, the women cash in. Bottom line is that the lascivious wolves from The Street are themselves run to financial ground. When they later find out they’ve been had, well, they’re afraid to admit they’ve been taken, considering wedding rings and humiliation are in play. The scheme is called “fishing.” And it takes proves hugely successful, so much so that Ramona and Destiny recruit some sisters to assist and that’s when some serious money begins to roll in. Think of it as transactional economics where the mark is played and reeled in. Meanwhile, Ramona and Destiny, who both have children, and the regulars, and Destiny’s grandmother, celebrate as an extended family. When not in the club, or hanging out with each other, they’re shopping, meaning serious shopping with matching Chinchilla coats and over the knee boots. And that’s the hustle. Ridiculously successful – until it isn’t when the stock market crash of 2008-09 causes the wolves of Wall Street to vanish. The sisters, now short on cash, are forced to get regular jobs. And when the cops show up things really got dicey. There was a lot of Oscar buzz around J-Lo’s performance, considered to be her best. articles.text: Buck Brannaman in Buck Perhaps part of the appeal of Buck is that from the first frame of this fine documentary we are looking at Buck Brannaman, the quintessential cowboy, an iconic image that has resonated for generations. Buck travels the U.S., conducting horse clinics for owners who have young colts who need breaking in, or horses that are a bit dysfunctional. Buck shares his approach, one that is firm and gentle and always respectful of the horse. He guides, cajoles and reassures, taking a skittish animal and transforming it. Think of his methods as Zen and the art of horse handling. The film also includes Buck’s tragic backstory. As youngsters, he and his brother were taken from state to state as trick ropers. When they weren’t performing at rodeos and fairgrounds, their father physically abused them until they were scarred. Buck is testimony to how one man, with grace and will and discipline, altered every aspect of his life. When young, he was simply looking to find a peaceful place where he didn’t feel threatened. What he found instead was his life’s work. To bear witness, to come, even briefly, to know this man is to understand how elusive it is to do what you love and thereby feel complete. To know that your insights, your knowledge, created out of years of experience, are significant and offer a certain wisdom regarding the human condition. Buck tells people firmly that horses mirror their owners, and how people treat their horses is how they treat others – family, friends and strangers. Buck is a remarkable film. Buck, Directed by Cindy Meehi. Documentary, with Buck Brannaman, Gary Meyers, Bib Frazier. 1 hr., 28 min. Released in 2011. Now streaming on Prime/ Apple tv

articles.text: First, I should disclose that I have never been a fan of the X-Men franchise, hence have missed all of its incarnations, dating back to 2000 when Logan/ Wolverine was first introduced. But when I saw the trailer for Logan I immediately sensed that this movie would be different. And indeed it is. The year is 2029 and most of the mutants are gone, hence Logan (Hugh Jackman) is essentially alone with the exception of Charles Xavier (Patrick Stewart) and Caliban (Stephen Merchant). They are hiding somewhere on the southern border, living in a converted metal-framed warehouse and converted, fallen water tower. The surrounding land is desert, the tones rust and sepia. Like Logan, Charles and Caliban, all is aged, worse for wear, and hard used. Meanwhile, Logan is lost in his personal rage constantly sipping from a bottle while working as a limo driver. It’s quickly evident that Logan is broken down, and his once superhero powers are slowly diminishing. What is also evident is that director James Mangold has adopted a western trope with Logan as the quintessential antihero. He is cynical, angry, foulmouthed, and insists that he only cares about getting Professor X, whose mind is fast eroding and prone to seizures, away to a boat where they can live out their days on the ocean. However, a young girl, Laura (Dafine Keen), is literally dropped on their doorstep and Logan finds himself, against his will, being her caretaker. She is, like him, a mutant, created in a lab, and as Logan learns, the feds and their Mad Max crew are out to find her and at all cost return her to the scientists. And so Logan morphs into a chase film with, admittedly, a high body count. But it’s not gratuitous. Nicely fitted into one scene, Charles and Laura are watching television and the movie is Shane. Of course, the similarities between Logan and Shane are irrefutable and the ending of Shane telegraphs the final scenes of Logan. This story is essentially a western, which makes it far more interesting than having to suspend one’s disbelief as 14 mutants/ superheroes confront all that CGI can create and then some. You don’t have to be a fan to enjoy or understand Logan. You just have to like movies in all of their forms. Logan. Directed by James Mangold. Starring Hugh Jackman, Patrick Stewart and Dafine Keen. 2 hrs., 15 min. Rated R. Hugh Jackman as Logan (Wolverine)

A cartoonist from an early age, once he began his studies at Princeton he abandoned cartooning. Following some time working in Bangkok, he entered law school at the University of Chicago. Although life as a litigation attorney was all-consuming, Phil tried to find time for creative activities. He wrote a few humor pieces, which attracted the attention of a book publisher. That led to a joke book, What You Don’t Know About Turning 50, and a sequel on turning 60. Sales to date are approaching 175,000 copies. “I knew I could write jokes, so I figured if I could combine that with drawing, I could become a cartoonist,” he said. “I was decent in art, but I needed to get a lot better, plus I had to develop a style… I’m still working on that.” He showed his early work to Phil Frank, the late cartoonist at The San Francisco Chronicle, who encouraged him. After trying for years to place his cartoons in The New Yorker, he decided to collaborate with one of the magazine’s veteran cartoonists, Kaamran Hafeez. “I sent him hundreds of gags over the past couple of years. He drew 50 or so of them and submitted them with his own cartoons.” Last year, two of them were published in The New Yorker. Even most of the “regular” cartoonists at the magazine get their work rejected over 95 percent of the time, Phil noted. Witte was recently elected by his peers to the National Cartoonist Society. His cartoons have been exhibited in San Francisco, Oakland, Minneapolis, London, Galway, Ireland, and most recently at Dominican University in San Rafael. pages.text: 20 Wednesday, January 18, 2023 The Musical Gourmet batting average was very high. The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet It always helps to be a participant. Some critics have had pens filled with vitriol. You can do that if you can also deliver the goods. A critic needs to have knowledge in all fields. While it might be exciting to see an athletic conductor, leaping on the podium like a great ballerina, the critic must look to see if the conductor is actually communicating with the musicians. Truth be told, many orchestra conductors don’t even know how to hold a baton. Sometimes the critic needs to be honest and admit culpability. Many years ago, I went to hear a famous cellist. Hearing him was a revelation. His command of the instrument was overwhelming, as was his emotional impact. I thought of the words of the comedian Flip Wilson who described playing like this as “the fury of 1000 jungle beasts.” Some years later, when I read how the composer wanted his music performed, I realized that the cellist was completely wrong…and so was my original opinion. By Will Adams Part 59 in a biweekly series: There is something comforting, reassuring, and just plain nice about seeing so many people out walking their dogs around town. It is impossible not to observe this at virtually any reasonable hour on any day of the year. Even the recent hard atmospheric river rains only seem to postpone dog Dog walking walking for a few hours. This illustrates one of the most obvious and valuable benefits of dog ownership: it gets humans outside and walking. Our friend the internet gives us confusing statistics, but it seems that about half of dog owners walk their best friends on a regular basis. From what I observe, it is easy to believe that the number of dog owners in Piedmont raises the average. This is good news for both species, human and canine, for a number of reasons. The vast majority of American humans, and about half of American canines are overweight or obese. This of course leads to heart problems, joint limitations, and digestive issues. Studies have shown that adults who regularly walk their dogs and benefit from the associated exercise are less likely than non-dog owners to Unclear On the Concept (actually witnessed outside Dracena Park) be afflicted with many physical problems from diabetes to cancer. Just like humans, obese dogs do not live as long as lean dogs. Plus, they suffer more heart problems and joint ailments that affect their quality of life. Dog walking has a positive impact on both canine and human mental and emotional health as well, as walking exercises the mind as well as the body. Neither dogs nor people like to be bored. Given something non-electronic and constructive to do like watching wildlife, exploring new paths, seeing other people with their pets provide great mental stimulation. Walking also releases excess energy and helps you sleep better at night. But what I find especially valuable is the enhanced sense of community fostered by this popular activity. People I have seen who respect and love another species, like most dog walkers, go out of their way to say hello and interact with other walkers on the streets, getting to know neighbors and strengthening the community we live in. Their goal is to produce wines of superior quality, leading them to Argentina to begin a new chapter. A 1990 vacation in Argentina was all it took. For third-generation winemaker Jean Bousquet, it was love at first sight. The object of the Frenchman’s desire: the Gualtallary Valley, a scenic, remote, arid terrain high in the Tupungato district of the Uco Valley in Argentina’s Mendoza region, close to the border with Chile. Here, with condors flying overhead and not a vine in sight, Bousquet discovered his dream terroir – an ideal location in which to nurture organically-grown wines. With altitudes ranging up to 5,249 feet, Gualtallary occupies the highest extremes of Mendoza’s viticultural limits. Fast-forward to the present: wine cognoscenti recognize it now as the source of some of Mendoza’s finest wines. Back then, it was virgin territory: tracts of semi-desert, nothing planted, no water above ground, no electricity and a single dirt track by way of access. Locals dismissed the area as too cold for growing grapes. Bousquet, on the other hand, reckoned he’d found the perfect blend between his French homeland and the New World (sunny, with high natural acidity and a potential for relatively fruit-forward wines). Nowadays, Domaine Bousquet produces 4 million liters a year and export 95% of its volume to more than 50 countries. Domaine Bousquet currently ranks in the top 20 Argentine wineries in terms of exports and is the leader in organic wine. I recently had the opportunity to taste three of the Domaine Bousquet wines. In addition to their high quality, • 2021 Domaine Bousquet Chardonnay, $18 Golden in color, the Bousquet Chardonnay has a nose that is robust with aromas of apple pears and oak as well as essence of citrus blossom and spices. Medium to full-bodied, the wine has a thoughtful complexity ending with lingering flavors of oak and a mineral flush. • 2021 Domaine Bousquet Cabernet Sauvignon, $18 Deep garnet-purple in color, the 2021 Caberrnet Sauvignon gives up notes of blackberries, cassis and chocolate with a waft of tobacco. Medium to full-bodied the palate is full of bright black fruit flavors with a solid foundation of fine-grained tannins, finishing long and juicy. • 2021 Domaine Bousquet Malbec, $18 The purple-colored 2021 Malbec is sensational for an entry level wine. It gives up an alluring nose of weed smoke, Asian spices, floral notes and raspberry. Layered smooth-textured, and plush, this is a mouth-coating effort that is ready to drink but that will continue to deliver satisfaction for another 5 or 6 years.

articles.text: Rain proved to be little deterrent to the Walking on Wednesdays group last week, January 11. On hand at the Exedra with umbrellas in hand, were Glen Tripp, Jim Kuo, Lois Price, Pat Keller, Tom Reese, Garrett Clifford, Meghan Bennett, Mark Davis, Sherry Jacobs, Claudia Lopez, Alicia Rivera, Priscilla Wanerus, and Dick Carter. Piedmont Post columnist Will Adams was also there to talk with the group about the architecture of Piedmont houses. A little atmospheric river last Wednesday morning didn’t deter an intrepid band of 14 members of the Walking on Wednesdays group from enjoying their weekly walk. The group has a mantra of “we walk rain or shine,” but not in thunder and lightning. Readers of the Piedmont Post saw photos the recent storms have caused around the city. They learned that the prior lightning had blown off the top half of a sequoia tree in the backyard of a home that borders Crocker Park. The Post article also told of flooding that had turned Witter Field into Witter Lake and other water damage around the city. Off they went, first to see the strong water flow in Bushy Dell Creek at the top of the Piedmont Park, then off to Crocker Park. The top half of the tree was gone, and its trunk had been torn open, exposing about 10 feet of the tree’s core. The remaining branches looked like they were part of a very large Charlie Brown Christmas tree. On the ground were tree chunks of splintered wood that could have filled a large fireplace. A light rain was falling, but the group was not ready to call it quits for the morning. They continued to King Avenue, where they noted a home that had been remodeled in a contemporary design. Will Adams offered some design comments and appreciated the use of wood and different levels of depth in the home’s exterior that provides visual interest. The group crossed Hampton and went to Farragut Avenue, admiring more beautiful homes along the way. At Crocker, the walkers stopped to talk about a Julia Morgan designed home on the corner and noted the owner has built a new home next door in a similar design that matches Morgan’s concept. They retraced their steps back to town center and the Community Hall parking lot. It had been about an hour, and almost two miles. The walkers saw some effects of the strong, recent rains and had a renewed respect for Mother Nature’s power. The group will continue to walk, rain or shine, but for sure not in lightning storms. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. Bushy Dell Creek was flowing at capacity through Piedmont Park during the rain on Wednesday.
articles.title: What’s a little rain among friends?

articles.text: Audrey Hepburn faces peril in Wait Until Dark The newly launched movie group, Second Friday Flix, opened with a screening on January 13 of Wait Until Dark, a thriller with Audrey Hepburn and Alan Arkin. More than 30 eager Piedmonters braved a driving rain last Friday to crowd into the Piedmont Recreation Department’s big front room to watch Audrey Hepburn face off against a trio of baddies. The occasion was the kickoff of the town’s newest attraction, Second Friday Flix, a movie-and-discussion event sponsored by the Recreation Department, where local film fans are invited to watch a movie together and chat about it afterward. Second Friday Flix is a monthly affair on the second Friday of the month from 12:30 to 3:30 p.m. at the Recreation Department, 358 Hillside Avenue. The group is open to anyone over age 18. There are no fees, and participants may attend on a drop-in basis by registering at https://bit.ly/3PJyxkP, or by contacting the Recreation Department at (510) 420-3070. Snacks and bag lunches are welcome. Attendees on opening day were treated to chewy squares of fudge, provided by movie-goer Pat Keller. The first showing was the 1967 suspense/thriller Wait Until Dark, starring Audrey Hepburn as recently blinded Susy Hendrix, whose husband, Sam (Efrem Zimbalist Jr.) has come into possession of a doll with packets of drugs sewn inside. The stash is a means to smuggle drugs into the United States. Neither Susy nor Sam know the truth about the doll, but three desperate criminals (Alan Arkin, Richard Crenna and Jack Weston) know all about the cache. They know who has it, too, and when Sam is away, they set their sights on innocent but resourceful Susy in her basement apartment. In order to discover the whereabouts of the doll, they try trickery, but when trickery fails, terror takes over, though Susy proves that a lone blind woman can be more than a match for a trio of toughs. Movie group member Darby Gragg capably introduced the film and led the discussion afterward. The audience largely approved, giving the movie many thumbs ups, especially for its performances, though there were some dissenters who pointed out plot weaknesses. The most notable objection was to Sam’s behavior at the climax, which some called “reprehensible” and “laughable” – it elicited groans. Nonetheless almost everyone thought Wait Until Dark provided an auspicious new offering. Second Friday Flix was organized and assembled by Dick Carter and volunteers Darby Gragg, Mike Gallant, Jasmine Cai, Gerry Gragg, and Bob Hall, with the assistance of Eva Phalen. Future screenings will be oriented to a different genre each month, such as comedy, romance, western, musical, drama. The next film, in the romance category, is 1971’s offbeat Harold and Maude, which will be screened on February 10 and presented by Mike Gallant. Attendees at Second Friday Flix’s premiere included: Alicia Bacon, Dick Carter, Helene Farber, Brenda Ferrero, Karin Fetherston, Darby and Gerry Gragg, Mike Gallant, Greg and Pat Keller, Bob and Madeline Hall, Jim and Kim Kellogg, Edith Lee, Claudia Lopez, Elene Manolis, Karen Murphy, Sarah Pearson, Karin Rawlins, Barbara Reding, Lisa Reynolds, Harriette Louie, Dorothy Shipp, Margaret Phillips, Noemi Alvarado and Mark Davis, Anne Alper, Swee Ling Chen, Albert Chen, Mike Henn, Alicia Rivera, and Melba Yee. articles.text: One of the best things about Piedmont is having interesting neighbors. In the Palm Drive enclave alone, to which my family had moved some 16 years ago, I have met CEOs whose companies disrupted their industries, academics from top universities, civil activists, musicians, and architects of renown. Still, I couldn’t help being surprised when I learned that a diminutive woman with bright blue eyes and a down-to-earth manner, with whom I occasionally discussed politics, held one of the toughest jobs in town. Meet Kim Hunter, Senior Deputy District Attorney for Alameda County. A native of Carmel, Kim attended Hastings College of the Law and served as an Alameda country DA for 37 years. In addition to working at the Family Justice Center, a collection of agencies and programs that provide services and support to victims of domestic violence, sexual exploitation, child abuse, and stalking, Kim also serves on the Bay Area Judicial Selection Advisory Committee and is a member of the Earl Warren American Inn of Courts. An avid reader of the Piedmont Post, Kim agreed to sit down with me over Christmas break and talk about her work, her community involvement, and her experience of living in Piedmont. A district attorney’s office is a tough place. You get to see the ugly side of life concealed from most people. How does one end up in the DA’s office? I was always interested in politics. When I started to analyze how people who ran for public office got there, I learned that most of them were lawyers. I went to law school, and though I spent the summer between my Kim Hunter with younger son Holden in front of the US Supreme Court building while attending American Inns of Court Celebration of Excellence in 2022. – Kim Hunter Alameda County Senior Deputy District Attorney first and second year at a boutique law firm, I saw myself more as a public defender. I wanted to defend people who were wrongfully accused. When I got an offer to join the Alameda County District Attorney office, I wasn’t sure: my leanings were against putting people in jail for no reason. During my first day in court, when I saw that 90 percent of defendants were black, I left the room and called my [African American] father. He told me, “Go back in there and make sure that the system is just and fair.” That’s what I’ve doing. Are there any specific qualities one must have to pursue a district attorney career? What’s the hardest part of your job? Kim Hunter with a photograph of her father, Robert Hunter, who taught PE for 39 years at Joaquin Miller Junior High School after retiring from the Army. You must be competitive to do this job. The mental game, the combination of tactical and strategic is what attracts me most. I’ve always played sports. At Cal I played field hockey–and though I was neither the tallest nor fastest, I was the most determined. So, of course I loved going to trial, loved the court room, loved public speaking. Being a DA really suited who I was. As for the toughest part. As a DA you have so much power, you must wield it very carefully, with great integrity and fairness. It’s a humbling task. If you’re going to charge someone over a serious crime, you don’t take that lightly. On the other hand, there are lots of people who lie, on both sides. Our job is to make sure that it’s not our side. To get to that point, you must do a lot of work with victims and the witnesses, and lots of follow-up. How do you create a safe space for them, empower them? What is your career highlight? It’s not the cases that I won, it’s the relationships I developed with the victims. Working at the Family Justice and seeing that the victims get the help they need has been truly rewarding. We’re trying to match our victim’s courage of speaking out and to assist them in doing whatever they need while remaining safe. Being a mentor is also very important to me. I love watching people grow, love seeing them navigate themselves through the office or doing the cases they’re most passionate about. articles.text: Larry Hu (left), Tanya Hu, Sandra Curach, Mona Jamieson, Elizabeth Wierzbianska, Gregory Jurin, Larry Singer, Janet Epstein; Martin Rossom in the space capsule at Chabot Space & Science Center. Not pictured: Patti Singer, Fred Pemberton, Jim Ayotte, and Irene Westler. The Piedmont Seniors plowed through rough weather conditions on their recent visit to the Chabot Space & Science Center located in the Oakland hills. The Center allows visitors to step into the role of a NASA scientist by getting a close-up look at cutting–edge technology of historic and future NASA missions. The NASA experience features some of the most fascinating items in space research and exploration, including space suits from the Mercury and Gemini missions, experimental heat shield technology, and even a fan blade from the world’s largest wind tunnel. Many of these items have never been on display to the public. On their visit the Seniors were able to explore pieces of NASA’s groundbreaking technology that make discovery possible, as well as embarking on hands-on challenges. At the NASA Ames Visitor Center the Seniors experienced an exhibition that brings to life the thrilling, challenging and inspiring process of scientific discovery by showcasing the real stories and people at NASA’s Ames Research Center. Visitors step into the role of a NASA scientist through an exhibit with more than 30 objects that show Ames’ past and future. One of the highlights of the trip was a visit to Chabot’s 70-foot dome-shaped Planetarium, where the show, “Lunaverse,” allowed thems to explore the nature of Earth’s Moon: its motion and phases, lunar and solar eclipses, tides, and the Moon’s origin. The story unfolds Piedmont Seniors enjoy lunch at the Paradiso restaurant after their visit to the Chabot Space & Science Center. as a conversation between a curious young child and the Moon — Luna — over the course of a night, from moonrise to moonset, all from the comfort of relaxing seats and a climate- controlled theater. Every Friday and Saturday night, weather permitting, the Chabot Observatory Deck is open to the public for free telescope viewing from 7:30 p.m. to 10:30 p.m. This is an opportunity to explore stars, planets, and various heavenly bodies through Chabot’s historic three large telescopes. During their excursion, the Piedmont Seniors were able to get close to spacecraft and explore how humans are expanding our boundaries by moving farther into the universe than ever before. With inspiration and content provided by NASA’s Ames Research Center, Cal Tech’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Planet, and SpaceX, the exhibit traces a journey through the cosmos ad what lies ahead. The seniors were also able to see out-of-this world objects, from the space program workhorse, an authentic 7K-OK Russian Soyuz Descent Module, to a Dove Cube Satellite Model, an example of the next generation of Nano satellites used to gather Earth imagery from space. After exploring the Center, the Seniors headed to Paradiso, a wonderful Italian restaurant located nearby in San Leandro. The camaraderie and delicious food more than made up for having endured the inclement weather. To learn more about the Piedmont Seniors, including future excursions, contact Janet Epstein, Seniors Coordinator, at jepstein@piedmont.ca.gov. Meetings are held on the fourth Wednesday of each month at the Piedmont Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue. The Seniors go on monthly excursions throughout the greater Bay Area.

articles.text: It’s your superpower. You’ve used it your entire life as a parent: Trouble shoot, problem solve, come up with the answers. As a grandparent, these skills may be more acutely honed than ever before. But now, with adult children who’ve become parents themselves, you need to develop a brand-new talent: become a listener. Remember when your name was called a million times a day? You were asked to find lost items, explain complex information, recommend how to do a new task, remember other family members’ birthdays, and in general explain to your children the way the world works. More often than not, these requests persisted until they were no longer little kids, but young adults. Now your child is a parent. You probably remember that you managed with Dr. Spock’s book, your mom (maybe), your pediatrician, and a couple of friends who had babies, too. Today, caring for a newborn or young child hasn’t really become more complex, but the input is much greater. It can feel like everyone is watching. You may hear your child struggling with all kinds of dilemmas during those first few years. Perhaps breast-feeding is a huge challenge as she returns to work and needs to pump regularly. Maybe the exhausted parents are torn between recommendations for sleep-training and attachment parenting. They may wonder if they should be promoting their child’s independence or making them feel super secure. And figuring out how to manage working from home when your child is sick can be a lot harder than it sounds. Other questions many new parents ask themselves are: • How do I know if I have picked a good daycare? • Is my baby sick or is it allergies? • Did I introduce peanuts early enough? • Should I read one book per night or three? • Did my baby have the right amount of tummy time? • When is it normal for toddlers to get out of diapers? • Does my child have to eat vegetables? • How can I help my child make friends? Every stage of parenthood has unique challenges and some may be tougher than others. When you see your child grappling with an issue, even when expressing true distress, it still may be the best choice to simply be a listener. Psychologists call this bearing witness, and it has been identified as being a tremendously healing action for those who are under stress or who have undergone a serious trauma. Is new parenthood traumatic? For some people the answer is yes. The drive to be successful at the raising of another human, the fear of making errors that may have lifelong consequences, and the terror of feeling judged to be inadequate in the role are enough to cause trauma in some cases. The next time your adult child shares with you how upset they are about something, listen and try to identify the message underlying the distress. Most likely it will be I’m scared, I’m tired, I’m confused. Sit quietly with them to bear witness to their experience without trying to solve the problem. What can you say instead? That sounds exhausting. I bet that was hard for you. You’re on the right track. I like the way you’re thinking about this. When you bear witness, you may find that your child comes to you more often with their life experiences (both positive and negative). People grow in strength and competence when they are provided with an empathetic listener instead of a problem solver, and we all want that for our children. Cynthia Kane is a board-certified, licensed genetic counselor with 25 years of clinical experience. A grandmother, Cynthia has a certificate in Grandfamily Leadership and is the founder of It’s Their Turn, which provides counseling, support, and education for grandparents. Online Grandparent Groups are forming now. Her website, https://itstheirturn.com/, provides a wealth of information and resources for grandparents. Cynthia can be reached at cynthia@itstheirturn.com

Dear MacMama: I just brought home a new MacBook Air, and the salesperson at the Apple store told me I can use iCloud to sync my items from my older computer to my new one. How does that work exactly? I don’t actually understand how iCloud works. – Oliver D., Piedmont Dear Oliver: Simply said, Apple’s iCloud is a storage service that can both store your files and sync them across all your devices. But there is much more to iCloud. We use it to sync contacts, reminders, calendars, and photos. We use it to store documents, folders, and passwords. If your computer has OS Catalina or later, when you turn on location services, you can use it to find misplaced iPhones, air pods, and Apple watches. If we use Air Tags, we can keep track of almost any item like wallets, keys, and anything to which we can attach an Air Tag. If your older Mac had OSX Yosemite or later, you can turn on iCloud Drive, enable “Desktop and Documents” and then all items on your desktop and in your “documents” folder will be stored in iCloud. They will still exist on your computer, and any other device in which you were signed in with the same Apple ID and have enabled iCloud Drive. This is great for people who have more than one device and need to keep their files in sync. So, for example, since I have iCloud enabled, if I work on a file in one computer, as soon as my other computer connects to the Internet, that file will be updated. And all my files are on both machines. If the operating system on your old computer is current enough and iCloud is enabled, you can set up the new computer, sign into iCloud, and these files will be downloaded onto your new computer. The same goes for photos, contacts and calendars. But this is not a complete solution for moving all your data over. And if you organize your mail into local folders, meaning the folders that exist in Apple Mail under the heading “On My Mac”, these will also not transfer over. So, in some cases, using Time Machine (assuming you have been backing up your old machine with Time Machine to an external drive) is a better way to transfer your data from an old machine to a new one. There are so many features in iCloud that it would take much more than this column to explain them all. Even if you use Time Machine on an external drive from your previous computer, in many cases, it is still prudent to enable iCloud to store and sync your desktop and documents. This acts as a cloud back up and makes these files accessible on your iPhone and iPad on the “Files” app, assuming the operating system on your device is current enough. A reach code is a local government ordinance that requires something in addition to the requirements of the state’s building code, and which can address all types of buildings: new buildings, existing buildings, single family buildings, multifamily dwellings, commercial buildings, and industrial buildings. If you care about your children and their education, you’re accepted here. I don’t feel “tolerated” because I am gay or of mixed racial background. I am a member of the community and love it. Whether I do something in the library or coach Little League, I participate. Piedmont is in fact much more diverse culturally and racially than people outside of town know. You maintain an impressive community calendar involvement. What are you focused on now? In addition to after-school sports activities, I am very involved with the career exploration program at the Piedmont Middle School. We’ve already welcomed Jeremy Bowers (Police Chief) and Teddy King (Mayor), with more interesting speakers on the horizon. We’re also planning an 8th grade trip to Washington DC this year. What do you do to relax? Do you watch crime shows? (Laughs) We used to watch Law and Order and then it got too negative, and we turned to comedy.
